title: Welcome, and what this blog is for
text:
“It is by logic that we prove, but by intuition that we discover.”
— Henri Poincaré, Science and Method

I started this blog for a simple reason. Every time I finally understand a piece of mathematics, the understanding arrives as a picture, not as a formula. The formula was always there; what changes is that I can suddenly see why it had to look that way. I wanted a place to hold onto those pictures before they fade.
So that is the spirit of everything here. I try to begin with the simplest version of an idea, the one small enough to fit in your head all at once, and grow it slowly until the general result feels less like a surprise and more like something you could almost have guessed. Only then do I write down the careful proof, because rigour is what lets you trust the picture later.
You will find the notes grouped into a few themes:

Pure — analysis, algebra, topology, number theory.
Applied — numerical methods, optimization, probability, differential equations.
Meta — paper reviews, study notes, and the occasional reflection like this one.

One promise I want to keep: every claim here is either proved, cited, or openly flagged as intuition rather than fact. When I get something wrong, and I will, I would rather fix it in the open than quietly hope no one noticed. Corrections are genuinely welcome through the issue link on each page.
If you want a feel for how a full note reads, the next one, on the Spectral Theorem, walks through a complete argument the way I like to tell them: a picture first, then the proof.

title: Gram–Schmidt: Straightening a Tangle of Vectors
text:
“A mathematician, like a painter or a poet, is a maker of patterns.”
— G. H. Hardy, A Mathematician’s Apology
Imagine a handful of vectors that all lean in roughly the same direction. They span some subspace, but they describe it badly: each one carries a little of every other one inside it, and it is hard to tell what is genuinely new about each. What we would love instead is a clean frame for that same subspace, a set of directions that are perfectly perpendicular and each of unit length, so that every vector in the space splits into independent, non-overlapping pieces. Gram–Schmidt is the simple, almost obvious procedure that builds exactly such a frame, one vector at a time. And once you see the picture, the QR decomposition falls out for free.

title: Gram–Schmidt: Straightening a Tangle of Vectors
text:
First, the picture
Start with the very first vector and do nothing clever at all. Just keep its direction; call that your first axis. The honest work begins with the second vector.
The second vector points partly along the first axis and partly away from it. The part along the first axis is redundant, since you already have that direction. So subtract it off. Concretely, cast a shadow of the second vector onto the first axis, the orthogonal projection, and remove that shadow. What survives points in a direction the first axis could never reach: it is perpendicular to the first by construction. That perpendicular remainder becomes your second axis.
Now the pattern repeats. Bring in the third vector, look at the shadow it casts on the plane already spanned by your first two axes, subtract that shadow, and whatever remains sticks out perpendicular to both. Keep going. At every step you take the next raw vector, strip away everything your existing axes already explain, and keep only the genuinely new direction left over. Normalize each remainder to unit length and you have an orthonormal frame.
That is the whole idea. Every formula below is just bookkeeping for “subtract the shadow.”

title: Gram–Schmidt: Straightening a Tangle of Vectors
text:
Writing it down
Let \(v_1, \dots, v_n \in \mathbb{R}^m\) be linearly independent, and write the inner product as \(\langle x, y\rangle = x^\top y\). The projection of a vector \(v\) onto a unit vector \(q\) is \(\langle q, v\rangle\, q\): the shadow’s length times the direction. Gram–Schmidt then reads
\[
u_k = v_k - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \langle q_j, v_k\rangle\, q_j,
\qquad
q_k = \frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k \rVert}.
\tag{1}\]
The sum is everything the earlier axes already account for; \(u_k\) is the leftover that they cannot. We normalize it to get the next unit axis \(q_k\).

title: Gram–Schmidt: Straightening a Tangle of Vectors
text:
It was QR all along
Look again at Equation 1 and rearrange it to express the original vector in terms of the new frame:
\[
v_k = \lVert u_k \rVert\, q_k + \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \langle q_j, v_k\rangle\, q_j .
\]
Read this as a recipe for rebuilding \(v_k\) out of the \(q\)’s. The crucial detail is which \(q\)’s appear: only \(q_1, \dots, q_k\), never any with a higher index. Each original vector lives entirely inside the axes built up to its own turn.
Stack the vectors as columns of a matrix \(A = [\,v_1 \mid \cdots \mid v_n\,]\) and the new axes as columns of \(Q = [\,q_1 \mid \cdots \mid q_n\,]\). The coefficients above assemble into a matrix \(R\), and because \(v_k\) uses no axis past \(q_k\), every entry of \(R\) below the diagonal is zero. We have landed on
\[
A = QR,
\tag{2}\]
with \(Q\) holding orthonormal columns and \(R\) upper triangular, its diagonal entries \(r_{kk} = \lVert u_k \rVert\) all positive. The geometric act of straightening a tangle of vectors and the algebraic factorization Equation 2 are the same thing seen from two sides.

title: Gram–Schmidt: Straightening a Tangle of Vectors
section: Why the frame is genuinely orthonormal
text:
Why the frame is genuinely orthonormal
It is worth checking that the picture delivers what it promises, rather than just feeling like it should.

Theorem 1 (QR by Gram–Schmidt) If the columns of \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) are linearly independent, then Equation 1 produces vectors \(q_1, \dots, q_n\) that are orthonormal and satisfy \(A = QR\) with \(R\) upper triangular and \(r_{kk} > 0\).


Proof. We argue by induction on \(k\) that \(q_1, \dots, q_k\) are orthonormal and span the same subspace as \(v_1, \dots, v_k\).
For \(k = 1\), \(q_1 = v_1 / \lVert v_1 \rVert\) is a single unit vector spanning the same line as \(v_1\), and \(\lVert v_1\rVert > 0\) because the columns are independent.
Assume the claim for \(k-1\). Form \(u_k\) as in Equation 1. For any earlier index \(i < k\), take the inner product with \(q_i\) and use orthonormality of the previous axes, \(\langle q_i, q_j\rangle = \delta_{ij}\): \[
\langle q_i, u_k\rangle = \langle q_i, v_k\rangle - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \langle q_j, v_k\rangle\,\langle q_i, q_j\rangle = \langle q_i, v_k\rangle - \langle q_i, v_k\rangle = 0 .
\] So \(u_k\) is perpendicular to every previous axis. It is also nonzero: if it vanished, Equation 1 would write \(v_k\) as a combination of \(q_1, \dots, q_{k-1}\), hence of \(v_1, \dots, v_{k-1}\), contradicting linear independence. Therefore \(q_k = u_k / \lVert u_k\rVert\) is a unit vector orthogonal to all earlier ones, and since \(u_k\) is \(v_k\) plus a combination of the previous axes, the spans still agree. The induction closes. Collecting the coefficients into \(R\) gives Equation 2, and \(r_{kk} = \lVert u_k\rVert > 0\). \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

title: Gram–Schmidt: Straightening a Tangle of Vectors
text:
Where the naive version breaks
Here the story takes a turn that pure mathematics alone would never warn you about. On paper, Equation 1 is flawless. On a computer, the order in which you subtract the shadows turns out to matter enormously.
There are two ways to organize the subtraction. Classical Gram–Schmidt computes every projection against the original vector \(v_k\) and removes them together. Modified Gram–Schmidt removes each shadow one at a time, always projecting the running remainder that is left so far. Algebraically the two are identical. In floating-point arithmetic they are not, because the modified version always works with the most up-to-date, mostly-perpendicular remainder, and so it never lets rounding errors pile up unexamined.
To see the gap, feed both versions a deliberately nasty matrix: the \(8 \times 8\) Hilbert matrix, whose columns are so nearly parallel that its condition number runs into the billions.

import numpy as np

def gram_schmidt(A, modified):
    m, n = A.shape
    Q = np.zeros((m, n))
    R = np.zeros((n, n))
    for k in range(n):
        v = A[:, k].copy()
        for j in range(k):
            # classical projects the original column; modified the running remainder
            R[j, k] = Q[:, j] @ (v if modified else A[:, k])
            v = v - R[j, k] * Q[:, j]
        R[k, k] = np.linalg.norm(v)
        Q[:, k] = v / R[k, k]
    return Q, R

n = 8
H = np.array([[1.0 / (i + j + 1) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)])
print(f"condition number of H: {np.linalg.cond(H):.2e}\n")

for name, modified in [("classical", False), ("modified", True)]:
    Q, R = gram_schmidt(H, modified)
    orthogonality = np.linalg.norm(Q.T @ Q - np.eye(n))
    reconstruction = np.linalg.norm(H - Q @ R)
    print(f"{name:9s}:  |Q^T Q - I| = {orthogonality:.2e}    |H - QR| = {reconstruction:.2e}")

Qh, _ = np.linalg.qr(H)   # numpy uses Householder reflections
print(f"{'numpy.qr':9s}:  |Q^T Q - I| = {np.linalg.norm(Qh.T @ Qh - np.eye(n)):.2e}")

condition number of H: 1.53e+10

classical:  |Q^T Q - I| = 1.42e+00    |H - QR| = 9.71e-17
modified :  |Q^T Q - I| = 3.62e-07    |H - QR| = 1.07e-16
numpy.qr :  |Q^T Q - I| = 1.46e-15


Both methods rebuild \(H\) from \(Q\) and \(R\) essentially perfectly, with \(\lVert H - QR\rVert\) down at roundoff. That is not where the danger lives. Look instead at \(\lVert Q^\top Q - I\rVert\), the honest test of whether the columns of \(Q\) really are orthonormal. Classical Gram–Schmidt scores around \(1\), meaning its “orthonormal” axes are nothing of the sort, they have collapsed back toward each other. The modified version holds the error near \(10^{-7}\), and the Householder-based routine in NumPy reaches full machine precision around \(10^{-15}\).
The lesson is not that Gram–Schmidt is wrong. It is that a formula can be exactly true and still be the wrong thing to type, because finite-precision arithmetic has a geometry of its own. When you actually need a stable orthonormal frame, reach for modified Gram–Schmidt or, better still, a Householder QR like the one inside numpy.linalg.qr. A careful account of all this lives in [1].

title: Gram–Schmidt: Straightening a Tangle of Vectors
text:
What to remember
The heart of Gram–Schmidt is a single move repeated: take the next vector, subtract the shadow your existing axes already explain, and keep the perpendicular remainder. That move, written out, is the factorization \(A = QR\), with the orthonormal frame in \(Q\) and the bookkeeping in an upper-triangular \(R\). The proof that the frame is truly orthonormal is a short induction resting on one cancellation. And the moment you run it, a quieter truth appears: on a real machine the naive ordering can throw the orthogonality away entirely, so the version you compute should be the modified one, or Householder if you can afford it.

title: About
text:
I’m Terry, a mathematics student who keeps getting pulled toward the place where pure theory, computation, and modelling meet. What I love most is the moment an abstract structure stops being a definition on a page and starts feeling like an object with a shape of its own.
A lot of my curiosity lives between worlds: topology and analysis on one side, network science, stochastic processes, optimization, and quantitative finance on the other. I keep this site as a long-term home for the notes, derivations, and small experiments I build while trying to understand these things properly.

title: About
text:
What you’ll find here
The notes here are written with three quiet ambitions:

to state definitions, theorems, and proofs precisely enough that I can trust them again months later;
to keep tracing the thread that connects abstract mathematics to computation and modelling;
to leave a reproducible record of the calculations, simulations, and half-formed ideas along the way.

Some posts are study notes on topics like topology, networks, probability, or optimization. Others are write-ups of a modelling project, a numerical experiment, or a paper I am slowly working through. Whatever the subject, the aim is the same: clarity, self-contained reasoning, and the occasional sense of wonder when an argument turns out to be more beautiful than it had any right to be.
Most of it is written for my future self. If it turns out to be useful to another student walking the same path, all the better.

title: Math Notes
text:
“The introduction of numbers as coordinates … is an act of violence.”
— Hermann Weyl, Philosophy of Mathematics and Natural Science

Most of the time, mathematics gets handed to us as a list of things to calculate. I have always been far more curious about the picture sitting underneath all that machinery: the reason a theorem has no choice but to be true, the quiet moment when a row of abstract symbols suddenly turns into something you can picture and almost touch.
This is where I work that out in the open. Each post starts from the simplest version of an idea I can find, builds up the intuition until the result feels inevitable, and only then writes down the formal proof. Where a picture or a few lines of runnable code make the idea easier to believe, I include them.
I write these mostly for the version of me who was once stuck on the very same thing. If you happen to be stuck there too, I hope they help.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
“Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different things.”
— Henri Poincaré
Here is a claim that sounds almost too clean to be true. Take any real symmetric matrix, no matter how tangled its entries look, and there is always a way to turn your head so that the transformation it describes does nothing fancy at all. It just stretches space along a set of perpendicular axes, each by its own amount. No shearing, no twisting, no mixing of directions. That is the whole content of the spectral theorem, and the rest of this post is about why space has no choice but to behave this way.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
First, the picture
Picture a linear map in two dimensions. In general it can do unpleasant things: it can rotate, it can shear a square into a slanted parallelogram, it can stretch more in one diagonal direction than another. A generic matrix really does mix your coordinate axes together.
Symmetry is the condition that quietly forbids all of that mixing, once you look from the right angle. The promise of the theorem is that for a symmetric matrix you can always find a fresh set of axes, still perfectly perpendicular to one another, in which the map becomes a pure diagonal stretch. Finding those special axes is the whole game, and they are exactly the eigenvectors.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Setting it up
Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, meaning \(A^\top = A\). Write the standard inner product as \(\langle x, y\rangle = x^\top y\). The single fact that powers everything below is that symmetry lets you slide \(A\) from one side of an inner product to the other:
\[
\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle \qquad \text{for all } x,y \in \mathbb{R}^n.
\tag{1}\]
This is worth a moment. It says \(A\) treats both slots of the inner product identically, a property called self-adjointness. Everything that follows is really Equation 1 wearing different costumes.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
The theorem

Theorem 1 (Spectral Theorem) If \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric, then there exist an orthogonal matrix \(Q\) (so \(Q^\top Q = I\)) and a real diagonal matrix \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\) such that \[
A = Q \Lambda Q^\top .
\tag{2}\] Equivalently, \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \(A\), and every eigenvalue is real.

Read Equation 2 from right to left and it tells the same story as the picture. The matrix \(Q^\top\) rotates you into the special axes, \(\Lambda\) does the honest diagonal stretching, and \(Q\) rotates you back. We reach it through two small observations.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Two small facts

Lemma 1 (Eigenvalues are real) Every eigenvalue of a real symmetric \(A\) is real.


Proof. Let \(Ax = \lambda x\) with \(x \neq 0\), where for the moment we allow \(\lambda\) and \(x\) to be complex. Write \(x^{*}\) for the conjugate transpose, so \(\langle x, x\rangle = x^{*}x = \|x\|^2 > 0\). Because \(A\) has real entries and \(A^\top = A\), it is Hermitian: \(A^{*} = A\). Now follow a single quantity, \(x^{*}Ax\), down two different paths: \[
\lambda\, \langle x, x\rangle = x^{*} A x = x^{*} A^{*} x = (Ax)^{*} x = \bar\lambda\, \langle x, x\rangle .
\] The first equality uses \(Ax = \lambda x\); the middle uses \(A^{*}=A\); the last uses \(Ax = \lambda x\) again, now inside the conjugated slot. Since \(\langle x, x\rangle > 0\) we may cancel it, leaving \(\lambda = \bar\lambda\). A number equal to its own conjugate is real. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)


Lemma 2 (Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal) If \(Ax = \lambda x\) and \(Ay = \mu y\) with \(\lambda \neq \mu\), then \(\langle x, y\rangle = 0\).


Proof. Slide \(A\) across the inner product using Equation 1: \[
\lambda \langle x, y\rangle = \langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle = \mu \langle x, y\rangle .
\] Therefore \((\lambda - \mu)\langle x, y\rangle = 0\), and since \(\lambda \neq \mu\) the only way out is \(\langle x, y\rangle = 0\). The special axes are automatically perpendicular, exactly as the picture demanded. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
Putting it together
We now assemble the theorem. The argument is an induction on the dimension \(n\), and each step leans on the two facts above.

Proof. The base case \(n = 1\) is immediate, since a \(1\times 1\) matrix is already diagonal. For the inductive step, Lemma 1 hands us a genuine real eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) with a unit eigenvector \(q_1\). Consider its orthogonal complement \(q_1^{\perp}\), the hyperplane of everything perpendicular to \(q_1\). Identity Equation 1 shows this hyperplane is \(A\)-invariant: if \(v \perp q_1\) then \(Av \perp q_1\) as well, so \(A\) never pushes you off the hyperplane. Restricted there, \(A\) is again symmetric but acts on a space of dimension \(n-1\), so the inductive hypothesis supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis of that smaller space. Adjoining \(q_1\) completes it to an orthonormal eigenbasis of all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Lining those vectors up as the columns of \(Q\) gives exactly Equation 2. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

For a complete and careful treatment, including the version for self-adjoint operators on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, see [1]. For the numerical side of the story, [2] is the classic reference.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
A numerical check
A proof tells you a decomposition must exist; it is a different kind of satisfying to watch it appear. Let us build a random symmetric matrix, ask the computer for its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and confirm that Equation 2 holds right down to floating-point roundoff.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 6
M = rng.standard_normal((n, n))
A = (M + M.T) / 2                      # force symmetry

eigvals, Q = np.linalg.eigh(A)         # eigh is built for symmetric matrices
Lambda = np.diag(eigvals)

reconstruction_error = np.linalg.norm(A - Q @ Lambda @ Q.T)
orthogonality_error  = np.linalg.norm(Q.T @ Q - np.eye(n))

print(f"eigenvalues (all real): {np.round(eigvals, 4)}")
print(f"|A - Q L Q^T| = {reconstruction_error:.2e}")
print(f"|Q^T Q - I|   = {orthogonality_error:.2e}")

eigenvalues (all real): [-2.0037 -0.988   0.2761  0.4913  1.5001  1.8151]
|A - Q L Q^T| = 1.62e-15
|Q^T Q - I|   = 1.39e-15


Both residuals sit around \(10^{-15}\), which is as close to zero as double-precision arithmetic ever gets. The eigenvalues come back real, the eigenvectors come back orthonormal, and the stretch-and-rotate story holds up.

title: The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
text:
What to remember
If you keep only three things from this note, keep these. Symmetry is really self-adjointness, the identity Equation 1, and that one fact is the engine of the entire proof. From it follow real eigenvalues (Lemma 1) and perpendicular eigenvectors (Lemma 2), which together build the orthonormal frame the theorem promises. And in practice, when you actually compute, reach for a symmetry-aware routine like eigh rather than the general eig; it is faster and it guarantees the real, orthogonal answer the mathematics says you deserve.
